title: Ancient & Medieval Shorts
chapters: Tutankhamun: the tomb that time forgot
Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War
The Library of Alexandria: what really happened

units.t: Ancient & Medieval Shorts.
In this episode: Tutankhamun: the tomb that time forgot, Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War and The Library of Alexandria: what really happened.
Part one. Tutankhamun: the tomb that time forgot.
He was a minor king who died as a teenager.
That is exactly why his tomb survived, and why its discovery in 1922 stunned the world.
The boy king.
Tutankhamun ruled Egypt for only about nine or ten years in the fourteenth century BC, coming to the throne at around eight or nine.
His father was very probably Akhenaten, the pharaoh who abandoned Egypt’s traditional gods to worship a single sun disc, the Aten.
The boy was originally named Tutankhaten, meaning living image of the Aten.
Early in his reign, guided by powerful advisers, the court restored the old gods, and his name was changed to Tutankhamun, honouring the god Amun.
He died at around eighteen or nineteen.
To later Egyptians, he was a footnote, and later kings even left his name off official lists.
Carter’s last season.
By the early twentieth century, most archaeologists believed the Valley of the Kings had given up all its secrets.
Howard Carter, an English archaeologist, disagreed.
Small finds bearing Tutankhamun’s name convinced him that the king’s tomb was still out there.
His sponsor, the fifth Earl of Carnarvon, was ready to stop paying by 1922, but Carter persuaded him to fund one final season.
On 4 November 1922, workers uncovered a stone step cut into the bedrock, leading to a sealed doorway.
On 26 November, Carter made a small hole and held up a candle.

Asked whether he could see anything, he later recalled replying that he could see wonderful things: gilded couches, statues, chests and chariots, in a room no one had entered for over three thousand years.
Robbed, but not emptied.
Tutankhamun’s tomb was not untouched.
Evidence showed that robbers broke in at least once, and probably twice, soon after the burial.
They took small, easily carried valuables such as oils and metal objects before officials found the break-in, tidied up and resealed it.
Then luck intervened.
Flood debris and the rubble and huts of workers digging later tombs, including that of Ramesses VI, buried the entrance, and it was forgotten.
The tomb itself was small, possibly a private tomb adapted in a hurry after his unexpected death.
Yet it held over five thousand objects, and recording, conserving and removing them took Carter and his team about a decade.
Gold, and much more.
The best known treasure is the funerary mask, made of gold inlaid with glass and semi-precious stones and weighing about ten kilograms.
The king’s body lay inside three nested coffins, the innermost of solid gold and weighing over a hundred kilograms, enclosed within a stone sarcophagus and four gilded wooden shrines.

But many of the most revealing objects were ordinary: chariots, bows, walking sticks, board games, linen underwear, sandals, jars of food and wine, and a lock of hair that belonged to his grandmother, Queen Tiye.
There were even two tiny mummified daughters, stillborn babies buried with their father.
Together these objects let historians see an Egyptian royal life in unusual detail.
The curse that wasn’t.
In April 1923, just months after the opening, Lord Carnarvon died in Cairo.
A mosquito bite, which he had accidentally nicked while shaving, became infected.
Newspapers competing for stories spread the idea of a pharaoh’s curse, and novelists such as Arthur Conan Doyle encouraged it.
No curse inscription was found in the tomb.
Howard Carter, who spent the most time inside, lived until 1939.
Later studies comparing people present at the opening with others found no sign that they died earlier.
How Tutankhamun himself died is still debated.
Scans and DNA studies have pointed to a broken leg, a foot deformity and evidence of malaria, but no single cause is agreed.
The key idea: Tutankhamun was a minor king who restored Egypt’s old gods and died at about eighteen or nineteen.
Part two. Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War.
A teenage peasant girl from a village in eastern France told a prince that God had sent her to save his kingdom.
Astonishingly, she very nearly did.
A very long war.
The Hundred Years' War actually lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with long truces.
At its heart was inheritance: English kings, descended from French nobility, held lands in France and claimed the French crown itself.
England won famous victories at Crécy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356 and Agincourt in 1415, where Henry V’s outnumbered army, with its longbowmen, defeated a much larger French force.
By the 1420s, France was in desperate trouble.
The Duke of Burgundy had sided with England, and the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 declared that the English king would inherit the throne, disinheriting the French heir, Charles, known as the Dauphin.
Paris and much of the north were under English and Burgundian control.
Voices and a test.
Joan was born around 1412 in Domrémy, in north-eastern France, to a farming family.
She could not read or write.
From about thirteen, she later said, she heard voices and saw saints, especially Michael, Catherine and Margaret, who told her to go to the Dauphin, drive out the English and see him crowned.
In early 1429, at around seventeen, she persuaded a local garrison commander to give her an escort, cut her hair short and rode in men’s clothing to the Dauphin’s court at Chinon.
Charles was cautious: she could be a saint, a fraud or an agent of the devil.
Churchmen at Poitiers questioned her for weeks and found nothing wrong in her faith or conduct.
The situation was desperate enough to take a chance.
Orléans and the coronation.
Orléans, the key to southern France, had been under English siege since late 1428.
Charles gave Joan armour, a banner and a place with an army bringing supplies.
She arrived at the end of April 1429.
She did not formally command, but her presence electrified soldiers and townspeople, and she pushed for bold attacks.
She was wounded by an arrow between neck and shoulder but returned to the fight.
On 8 May the English abandoned the siege.
More victories followed, including Patay in June.
Joan then urged Charles to make the dangerous journey to Reims, the traditional site where French kings were crowned.
On 17 July 1429 he was crowned Charles VII, with Joan standing nearby holding her banner.
Captured and tried.
After the coronation, Joan’s fortunes turned.
An attack on Paris failed, and the king grew more interested in negotiation than war.
In May 1430, while defending Compiègne, she was pulled from her horse and captured by Burgundian soldiers, who sold her to the English.
There is no evidence that Charles made any serious attempt to rescue her.
In 1431 she was tried for heresy in Rouen by a Church court led by Pierre Cauchon, a bishop allied with the English.
They needed her condemned, since that would suggest Charles had been crowned with the devil’s help.
The records show an illiterate young woman answering trick questions from learned men with remarkable sharpness and courage.
Burned, then vindicated.
One major charge was that she wore men’s clothing, which her accusers treated as a sin against divine law.
Under pressure she signed a statement renouncing her claims and agreed to wear women’s dress, but days later she resumed men’s clothing, and the court declared her a relapsed heretic.
On 30 May 1431, in the market square of Rouen, she was burned at the stake.
She was about nineteen.
Within a generation, the war she had helped turn ended, as French armies took back Normandy and Gascony.
By 1453, England held only Calais.
A retrial authorised by the Pope declared the original verdict null in 1456.
Joan was made a saint in 1920 and is a patron saint of France.
The key idea: By the 1420s France was close to defeat, with English and Burgundian forces holding Paris and the north.
Part three. The Library of Alexandria: what really happened.
It is the most famous lost library in history, supposedly destroyed in a single catastrophic fire.
The truth is slower, stranger and more of a warning.
A library for the world.
After Alexander the Great died, his general Ptolemy took Egypt and made Alexandria his capital.
Early in the third century BC, Ptolemy I or his son Ptolemy II founded the Mouseion, a temple to the Muses that worked as a research institute, and with it the Library.
The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to outshine Athens as the centre of Greek culture, so they paid scholars to live, work and dine together at royal expense.
The aim was bold: collect every important book written in Greek, plus translations of works from other cultures.
A later tradition says the Hebrew scriptures were first translated into Greek there, producing the Septuagint.
Hungry for books.
The physician Galen, writing centuries later, told two stories.
Ships arriving in the harbour were searched for books, which were copied; the owners received the copies and the Library kept the originals.
And Ptolemy III borrowed the official Athenian texts of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, left fifteen talents of silver as a deposit, then kept the originals and forfeited the money.
These tales may be exaggerated.
The size is just as uncertain.
Ancient writers give figures from about forty thousand to seven hundred thousand scrolls, often long after the fact, and duplicates and multi-scroll works muddle any count.
Its main rival was Pergamon, in modern Turkey.
The scholars.
Eratosthenes, one of its chief librarians, estimated the circumference of the Earth by comparing the angle of the Sun's shadow at Alexandria and at Syene, far to the south, on the same day.
His result was remarkably close to the true value, though historians debate how close because his units of length are uncertain.
The poet Callimachus compiled the Pinakes, a huge catalogue of Greek authors and works, often called an ancestor of the library catalogue.
Zenodotus and Aristarchus produced careful editions of Homer by comparing different copies to remove errors.
Alexandria also became a great centre of medicine, mathematics and astronomy.
Caesar's fire.
The most famous story of the Library's destruction involves Julius Caesar.
In 48 BC, besieged in Alexandria during the civil war involving Cleopatra and her brother, Caesar set fire to ships in the harbour.
Several ancient writers say the blaze spread and burned books, and Seneca mentions forty thousand lost.
But the sources disagree about what burned.
Some historians think the fire mainly destroyed warehouses near the docks holding scrolls awaiting export or cataloguing, not the Library itself.
What is clear is that scholarly life continued.
The geographer Strabo worked in the city a couple of decades later and wrote about the Mouseion, without mentioning a destroyed library.
A slow fade.
As early as 145 BC, Ptolemy VIII expelled many intellectuals, including the head librarian Aristarchus.
Under Roman rule royal patronage vanished, and in the AD 270s fighting under Aurelian devastated the palace quarter where the Library probably stood.
A quieter enemy was damp coastal air, which rotted fragile papyrus scrolls unless they were recopied.
A library that loses its funding and staff loses its books without any fire.
Later writers blamed convenient villains.
The AD 391 destruction of the Serapeum, and the murder of Hypatia in 415, did not destroy the Library.
The tale of Caliph Umar burning books in 642 first appears over five centuries later, and most historians reject it.
The key idea: The Ptolemies founded the Library in the early third century BC, inside a royal research institute called the Mouseion.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What changed in Egyptian religion early in Tutankhamun’s reign?
Answer. The old gods were restored after Akhenaten.
Question two. What did the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 declare?
Answer. The English king would inherit the French throne.
Question three. What was the Ptolemies' ambitious aim for the Library?
Answer. To gather every important Greek book and translations.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
